content:
It’s Tuesday evening. I only want to know one thing: do my two kids have homework for tomorrow?
In Denmark that question goes through Aula, the platform every public school and most daycare centres use to talk to parents. In Aula it goes like this. First MitID, the national digital ID. Then the front page with posts from the school, from after-school care and from the class. Then I find the widget with the weekly plan, which opens Meebook, one of the vendors schools pick for lesson plans. The homework is in there, mixed in with the teachers’ notes about what the class is working on that week. And then I do the whole thing again for child number two.
It’s easy to get annoyed with Aula. I have been. But the more I’ve looked at it, the more I’ve come to think that Aula has been given a job nobody can do.
For everyone is for no one # Aula has to work for every parent with a child in public school, and for a large share of daycare. For teachers, pedagogues and heads of school. For pupils from the youngest classes up. On a phone on the bus and on a computer at the office. For parents with one child and parents with four. For divorced parents who need to see the same thing from two addresses. For people who are dyslexic, and people whose first language isn’t Danish.
And Aula has to do all of it at once: messages, calendar, timetable, drop-off and pickup times, reporting a child sick, posts, photos and consent forms. On top of that come the widgets from whichever vendors the school has chosen. The weekly plan lives in Meebook at one school and in Min Uddannelse or EasyIQ at the next.
Every single feature is something someone needs. And that same feature is noise to everyone else. For parents of a toddler in daycare, what matters is drop-off and pickup, and photos. For me, with two kids in lower secondary, it’s homework and substitute lessons. For a teacher it’s something else entirely.
A user interface that has to be for everyone ends up being a little for everyone and not really for anyone. That isn’t bad craftsmanship. It’s a sum that doesn’t add up. You cannot make one front page that is the right front page for all of those people.
So Aula can’t win. Whatever it does, it is too much for some and too little for others.
My own way in # So what I was missing wasn’t a better Aula. I was missing a view into it that shows only what I need.
Luckily, others have done the hard part. Aula has no official API to build on, but scaarup/aula has been pulling data out of Aula into Home Assistant for years. And Casperjuel/aula-mcp has rebuilt the entire MitID login without a browser. Both are open source, and without them I couldn’t have built this in an afternoon.
I reuse the login from aula-mcp and wrote the rest as a module for Nushell, the shell I use for almost everything. Every command returns a table:
> aula lektier ╭───┬───────┬───────────┬───────────┬──────┬─────────────────────────╮ │ # │ child │ date │ subject │ kind │ text │ ├───┼───────┼───────────┼───────────┼──────┼─────────────────────────┤ │ 0 │ A │ Wed 28/10 │ English │ task │ 6 grammar exercises │ │ 1 │ O │ Wed 28/10 │ Danish │ task │ Read up to chapter 4 │ │ 2 │ O │ Thu 29/10 │ Maths │ task │ Hand in: weekly task 3 │ ╰───┴───────┴───────────┴───────────┴──────┴─────────────────────────╯ (Lektier is Danish for homework. Some of the commands kept the Danish words Aula itself uses.)
There are commands for the things I actually use: aula lektier, aula ugeplan, aula calendar, aula presence, aula threads and a few more. Because the result is a table, I can ask the questions Aula has no button for. Which lessons have a substitute this week?
aula calendar --week | where status == substitute | group-by child Aula will never get that button. It only matters to some of us, and for everyone who doesn’t need it, it’s just one more button.
One page for a tick # The terminal works for me, but not at the dinner table. So on top of the module I built a small web page that runs on my own machine. It shows the two kids side by side, A on the left and O on the right, with their homework for this week and next.
My homework page (in Danish). Names are shortened, and homework from days that have passed stays red until it is done. Next to each piece of homework there is a button: Mark done.
That is the only new thing the page does, and it’s exactly what Aula has no place for. In Aula, homework is a message from the teacher. On my page it is also a task that gets done. If homework from an earlier day is done, it disappears. If it isn’t, it stays, under a red heading. Anything that turned up since yesterday is marked “new”.
The division of labour is simple. Aula owns the homework. Every half hour the page fetches it and stores a snapshot. The page owns only the ticks, and it stores them as a log of what happened: done, undone, done again. That log is cross.stream, and the server is http-nu, both written by Andy Gayton. The page itself is rendered on the server and updates live, so it is the same on the phone and on the computer.
Everything runs on my own machine. The MitID access sits in my Mac’s keychain, and the kids’ school data never leaves the house.
Give us data, not a better front page # I don’t think the answer is for Aula to design its way out of this. It can’t be done. Every time someone gets the feature they were missing, the front page gets a little heavier for everyone else.
If something has to be for everyone, maybe the best user interface isn’t a user interface. It could be proper access to the data: a documented API, so parents, associations, apps and people like me can build the small way in that fits their own everyday life. Mine is two columns and a tick. Another parent’s would look completely different.
Until then, it’s enthusiasts like the people behind scaarup/aula and aula-mcp who keep the door ajar. They do it in their spare time, and every time Aula bumps its API version, they have to patch things up. That’s a fragile foundation for something every school parent in the country is required to use.
Have you built your own way into Aula, or would you like to? Then send me an email. I’d love to hear what your front page would show.
title: Aula can't win

content:
I can’t opt out of Aula. If I have children in a Danish public school, that’s where the school writes to me, where I report them sick, and where I find the weekly plan. Except the weekly plan isn’t even in Aula. It lives in Meebook, Min Uddannelse or EasyIQ, depending on what the school has picked. I can’t opt out of those either.
I’m fine with that. A shared channel between school and home makes sense, and someone has to choose it.
But when someone decides that I must use a particular portal, I think they owe me something in return: an official way to get to my own data. Not just through their screen, but through an API.
This isn’t a theoretical wish # In Aula can’t win I wrote about my small app that shows my two kids’ homework side by side with a tick next to each item. It works. But look at what it rests on.
Aula has no official API. What I and others build on is the API Aula’s own app and website use. It isn’t documented, and nobody has promised it will keep working. It changes version a couple of times a year, and then the unofficial tools break until someone works out what changed.
Login goes through MitID, the Danish national digital ID. For a program to log in as me, the people behind aula-mcp have had to rebuild the entire MitID flow in code. It’s impressive work. And it can be stopped by bot protection that can’t tell a parent with a script from an attacker.
The homework sits with a third vendor. Aula issues a short-lived ticket for Meebook, and Meebook then wants a particular header containing my MitID username, or it won’t answer. You only find that out by watching over the shoulder of Aula’s website while it talks to Meebook. Someone has had to do that for every single vendor.
All of it is done by volunteers in their spare time. It’s not a foundation you can build anything lasting on. And it shouldn’t be necessary.
An API is also the safest option # The objection I hear most is security. These are children’s data, after all.
But that’s exactly the point. Right now, the only way a tool can read my kids’ homework is by getting full access to my Aula login. The same login that can read every message, including the sensitive ones, and report my children sick. A tool that only needed to see the weekly plan gets the keys to the whole house.
An official API could do the opposite. It could give me a key that can only read homework and timetables, and can’t write anything. A key I can see in a list and revoke with one click. That’s how most large services work when you connect other programs to them. It’s far safer than what people do today, because they have no other choice.
And an API doesn’t open up anything new. It shows exactly what I can already see when I log in. The only difference is that a program reads it instead of my eyes.
The law doesn’t give it to us # You’d think the GDPR would solve this. It gives a right to data portability: to receive your data in a machine-readable format. But that right doesn’t apply when a public authority processes data to carry out a task in the public interest. And that’s exactly what a municipality does in Aula.
The right of access still applies, but it gets me a printout, not access I can build on. So if we want APIs for the portals we’re required to use, they won’t come by themselves. Someone has to demand them. That’s true in Denmark, and it’s true anywhere else in the EU.
Who can do something # Aula is bought by Denmark’s municipalities together, and it’s the schools and municipalities that pick Meebook and the others. Whoever pays can set requirements.
A requirement for an official API could be in every contract with a vendor of a portal citizens have to use. Yes, it costs something to build and maintain. But the vendors already have an API, because that’s what their own app talks to. What’s missing is documenting it, promising to keep it stable, and giving citizens a proper key.
What I’d ask for isn’t much:
Documentation. Which data, which fields, what they mean. Stability. Changes announced well ahead, and old versions not shut down overnight. Scoped keys. Read access to what I choose and nothing else. Visible and easy to revoke. The same rules for vendors. Meebook, Min Uddannelse, EasyIQ and the others should meet the same bar when they sit behind a portal we can’t opt out of. And it isn’t only about school. It applies everywhere the public sector has decided we must be.
What we’d get out of it # When data is available, people build things no portal would ever prioritise. A homework list with ticks for two kids. A reminder when there’s a substitute in the first lesson. An overview for divorced parents that gathers everything in one place. Read-aloud for the dyslexic parent. A translation for the parent whose first language isn’t Danish.
Aula doesn’t have to build any of them. Aula just has to stop standing in the way.
The public sector has already shown it can do this. Denmark shares addresses, company registration numbers and other core data as open data, and a lot of good has been built on top. The only question is whether we may also build on the systems we’re required to use, with our own data.
I think the answer should be yes. If you agree, tell your municipality and your school board. And if you’d like to know more about what it takes technically, send me an email.
title: Forced in, locked out

content:
When someone shows me an AI system, I don’t start by asking about the model or the platform. I ask four questions. I’ve asked them so many times by now that I’ve started calling them the Kiil principles for AI.
They sound simple, and they are. Still, it’s surprising how few people can give a sharp answer. I’ve had to rebuild my own systems more than once because they couldn’t either.
1. Which parts are rules, and which are model? # A language model is good at judgement. It can read a sloppy email, summarise a report and suggest a phrasing. It’s bad at rules. It can’t be trusted to calculate VAT, keep a deadline or remember that a customer in arrears doesn’t get credit.
Rules belong in code that runs the same way every time and can be tested. If your prompt says “always remember to”, you’ve written down a wish, and nobody can test a wish.
In my own job application system the model may write the cover letter freely. In the CV it may only cut. Every line it proposes is compared word for word with my master CV, and if a single one differs, the CV isn’t written at all. So the model can’t invent experience I don’t have. The prompt asks it not to, but it’s the code that makes sure.
2. What happens when the model gets it wrong? # Because it will. The only question is whether anyone notices.
The dangerous failures are the quiet ones. A model that doesn’t know the answer answers anyway. A broken integration reports “no new data”, and that looks exactly like a slow day. I once had a data source return zero results for four days without anything raising a flag.
So validate before you write. Stop the process rather than return an empty answer that looks like a real one. And remember that a check you’ve only ever seen pass is a check you don’t know works. You need to have seen it fail at least once.
One of the best tricks I know is to ask the same question twice: once with rules and once with a model. Where they agree, the case moves on. Where they disagree, a human takes a look.
3. Can you show me afterwards why the system made a particular decision? # I’m not asking what the model said. I’m asking why the system did what it did.
A log of prompts and responses is a transcript of a conversation. An audit trail follows the decision: which case it was, what data went in, which rule kicked in, what the outcome was, and who approved it.
It sounds like bureaucracy until a customer complains or the auditor calls. In my case, the trail is what revealed that an automatic reminder was about to chase me for something I’d already done.
The EU AI Act requires logging for high-risk systems. But law or no law, management can’t take responsibility for something it can’t see.
4. Which actions require a human, and why those in particular? # “A human approves everything” lasts about three weeks. After that the approval is a click nobody reads, and you have a rubber stamp with a log file behind it.
Humans belong in two places: where the system knows it’s unsure, and in front of actions that can’t be undone.
My test is a single question. Can it be reversed? A draft on my own disk I can simply make again, so that runs on its own. An application that has been sent can’t be called back, so there the system waits for me. How hard a step is doesn’t decide it.
The platform comes later # Notice that none of the four questions is about which model, cloud or vector database the solution runs on. That has to work too, of course, but it’s an operations job, and it can be solved.
If someone can answer the four questions sharply, the rest is detail. If they can’t, no platform will save them.
Take them with you the next time you buy, hire or build something with AI. And feel free to ask them of me.
I’ve written a longer version with more examples (in Danish) on docujai.com: Platformen er ikke arkitekturen. If you’d like help asking these questions of your own systems, send me an email.
title: The Kiil principles for AI

content:
I will use:
Nushell Custom Completions Nushell Custom Commands Nushell Modules Nushell builtins Yeah, it kinda looks like I will use Nushell 🐘 a lot.
But the heavy email lifting will be done by the excellent Himalaya pimalaya/himalaya: CLI to manage emails.
The parsing of my vcard contact files is done with the Nushell formats plugin: nu_plugin_formats - crates.io: Rust Package Registry
Let’s get started:
I create a file called numail.nu and put it in my modules folder.
In this file I start by defining a function, or Custom Completion, that will return a list of all contacts with an email address.
def recipient [] { { options: { case_sensitive: false, completion_algorithm: fuzzy, }, completions: (glob /home/lk/.contacts/Google/default/*.vcf # these are vcard files for contacts | open ...$in | get properties | each { transpose -r } # requieres nu_plugin_formats | flatten | where EMAIL? != null and FN? != null | select FN EMAIL | insert recipient { format pattern r##'{FN} <{EMAIL}>'## } | get recipient ) } } You can read more about Custom Completions here: Custom Completions | Nushell
I can now select from this list of contacts in a Custom Command like so:
export def numl [ ...recipient: string@recipient --attachment (-a): string --from (-f): string = "xxxxxxx@gmail.com" --greeting (-f): string = "Kære " --signature (-s): string = "\n\nMed venlig hilsen,\nLennart" --subject (-s): string = "Vigtigt" ] { let message = $in let recipient = $recipient | str join " " | parse "{name} <{to}>" let eml = $"From: ($from)\nTo: ($recipient.to | to text --no-newline)\nSubject: ($subject)(char nl)(char nl)($greeting)($recipient.name | to text --no-newline)(char nl)(char nl)($message)($signature)( if ($attachment | is-empty) {} else {$'(char nl)(char nl)<#part filename=($attachment)><#/part>'} )" $eml | ^himalaya template send $in # requieres CLI to manage emails https://github.com/pimalaya/himalaya } I place the above Custom Command, together with the Custom Completion from, earlier in a Nushell Module - just a file called numail.nu.
I then load the module like so:
use numail.nu *
Now in my Nushell REPL I have the numl Custom Command at my disposal. And because of Custom Completions I can simply write:
numl and then the first few characters in a recipient’s name and then the tab key and Nushell will provide me with a simple menu to choose from among my contacts with names containing the few characters I wrote.
The email message itself is “piped” in like so.
"Det er bare en test" | numl Lennart <xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx@gmail.com> Message successfully sent!
Bonus:
If you would prefer to write the message of the email in your editor instead of directly on the command line, use the following:
vipe --suffix eml | numl Lennart <xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx@gmail.com> This requires that you have the moreutils package installed.
Now that I can send mails directly from the command line, sending mails becomes scriptable. And when something is scriptable it also becomes easier to automate and to integrate with artificial intelligence.
But that is a subject for another article.
title: Send email from the command line with Nushell and Himalaya

content:
Let’s say I have:
╭───┬──────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────╮ │ # │ navn │ branchekode │ hovedkontor │ ├───┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┼─────────────┤ │ 0 │ Maersk │ Transport og logistik │ København │ │ 1 │ Novo Nordisk │ Lægemidler │ Bagsværd │ │ 2 │ Danske Bank │ Finans og bank │ København │ ╰───┴──────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────╯ And I would like to add a column with contact information.
I can easily do that with Nushell and a large language model:
open virksomheder.json | insert kontakt { $in | format pattern "har du et bud på kontakt email til {navn} returner kun en emailadresse og returner kun selve emailadressen" | cer complete } And then suddenly we have:
╭───┬──────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────────────┬────────────────────────────╮ │ # │ navn │ branchekode │ hovedkontor │ kontakt │ ├───┼──────────────┼───────────────────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────────┤ │ 0 │ Maersk │ Transport og logistik │ København │ contact@maersk.com │ │ 1 │ Novo Nordisk │ Lægemidler │ Bagsværd │ info@novonordisk.com │ │ 2 │ Danske Bank │ Finans og bank │ København │ kundeservice@danskebank.dk │ ╰───┴──────────────┴───────────────────────┴─────────────┴────────────────────────────╯ Here it is the `format pattern’ in Nushell which makes it easy to create dynamic prompts where certain words in the prompt are replaced with the right word according to the given context.
In this case, as you can see, I take the name of the company from the navn column and insert it at the proper position in the prompt to create the new kontakt column.
title: Use `format pattern` in Nushell to create dynamic LLM prompts

content:
Jeg har længe brugt AI til at lave notitser og til at lave kortere analyser. På det korte notits-format gør kunstig intelligens sig rigtigt godt, særligt hvis man fodrer den med rigelige mængder tekst at forholde sig til.
Analyserne er heller ikke dårlige. I hvert fald ikke i forhold til at belyse nævnte aspekter fra mange vinkler. Ægte selvstændighed i analyserne kniber det dog en del med.
Min konklusion på LLM’er for øjeblikket:
Kunstig intelligens i sin nuværende form excellerer når
tekst skal sammenfattes. der skal fremsøges relevante passager eller data (gerne med RAG). når kortere brudstykker af tekst skal “foldes ud” og eksemplificeres. Men der findes også områder hvor det måske er meningsløst at bruge kunstig intelligens.
Et meget stort område indholdsområde er opinion. Læserbreve, klummer, debatindlæg, med mere. For slet ikke at tale om de mange visuelle influencere på de forskellige videoplatforme.
Mennesker har øjensynligt at behov for at give udtryk for deres holdninger.
Men giver det mening at lade en kunstig intelligens udtrykke sin “holdning”?
Ikke rigtigt. Der er vi i hvert fald ikke endnu.
Men det betyder ikke at kunstig intelligens ikke har nogen rolle at spille i forhold til opinionsstof.
Kunstig intelligens kan for eksempel bruge til at assistere ordblinde, så de lettere kan udtrykke deres holdninger på skrift.
Men der er også en anden måde man kan bruge kunstig intelligens på i forhold til opinion.
Som sparringspartner!
Du kan skrive op imod en kunstig intelligens.
Bede den påpege mangler i din argumentation.
Bede den supplere eller bidrage med andre perspektiver.
Du kan få den til at give dig en liste over typiske modargumenter.
Du kan endda, med lidt tekniske snilde, sætte to kunstige intelligenser til at diskutere med hinanden med udgangspunkt i dine egne holdninger så der opstår en dialektik.
Eller du kan bede den kunstige intelligens stille spørgsmål til dit debatindlæg og på sokratisk vis komme frem til et bedre resultat.
I sidste ende er det din egen kreativitet som sætter grænserne for hvad kunstig intelligens kan bruges til.
title: Giver det mening at lade en kunstig intelligens give udtryk for sine holdninger 🤔

Since Large Language Models are trained on vast amounts of human text and since human text is reflecting human language which again is reflecting human psychology, it should be possible to use LLMs to find patterns in text that correspond to human emotional states.
In a recent tragic murder that has received enormous attention the world over, a 26 year old man by the name of Luigi Mangione is suspected of having killed CEO of UnitedHealthcare Brian Thompson.
Luigi Mangione allegedly was in possesion of a “manifesto” at the time of his apprehension by police.
I asked OpenAIs latest and greatest model o1-preview to analyze the manifest.
But first the manifesto by itself:
To the Feds, I’ll keep this short, because I do respect what you do for our country. To save you a lengthy investigation, I state plainly that I wasn’t working with anyone. This was fairly trivial: some elementary social engineering, basic CAD, a lot of patience. The spiral notebook, if present, has some straggling notes and To Do lists that illuminate the gist of it. My tech is pretty locked down because I work in engineering so probably not much info there. I do apologize for any strife of traumas but it had to be done. Frankly, these parasites simply had it coming. A reminder: the US has the #1 most expensive healthcare system in the world, yet we rank roughly #42 in life expectancy. United is the [indecipherable] largest company in the US by market cap, behind only Apple, Google, Walmart. It has grown and grown, but as our life expectancy? No the reality is, these [indecipherable] have simply gotten too powerful, and they continue to abuse our country for immense profit because the American public has allwed them to get away with it. Obviously the problem is more complex, but I do not have space, and frankly I do not pretend to be the most qualified person to lay out the full argument. But many have illuminated the corruption and greed (e.g.: Rosenthal, Moore), decades ago and the problems simply remain. It is not an issue of awareness at this point, but clearly power games at play. Evidently I am the first to face it with such brutal honesty.
I asked o1-preview to analyze that, no further instructions, simply “analyze this”. The result is:
The provided text appears to be a written statement or manifesto addressed to federal authorities (“To the Feds”) by an individual who has undertaken some form of direct action against entities within the U.S. healthcare system. The tone, content, and context suggest a complex mix of personal conviction, ideological motivation, and a desire to justify actions taken.
Key Observations:
Address to Federal Authorities:
The author directly addresses federal agents, indicating an awareness that their actions will attract law enforcement attention. By stating “I’ll keep this short” and “To save you a lengthy investigation,” the author seems to be attempting to control the narrative or expedite the investigative process. Admission of Sole Responsibility:
The explicit statement “I wasn’t working with anyone” emphasizes that the author acted alone. This could be an attempt to prevent authorities from implicating others or to claim full responsibility for the actions taken. Methods Employed:
References to “elementary social engineering,” “basic CAD,” and “a lot of patience” suggest that the author used manipulation techniques, computer-aided design, and meticulous planning. This indicates a certain level of technical proficiency and strategic thinking. Evidence and Documentation:
Mention of a “spiral notebook” containing “straggling notes and To Do lists” that could “illuminate the gist of it” points to physical evidence that might be discovered. The author notes that their technology is “pretty locked down,” implying efforts to secure or hide digital evidence. Justification and Ideological Motivation:
The author expresses remorse for any “strife of traumas” caused but insists “it had to be done,” highlighting a belief that the ends justify the means. Describing the targets as “parasites” who “had it coming” reflects deep-seated resentment and dehumanization of those entities. Critique of the U.S. Healthcare System:
Highlights the disparity between the high cost of healthcare in the U.S. and its comparatively low life expectancy ranking (#42). Specifically mentions “United,” likely referring to UnitedHealth Group, indicating it as one of the largest companies and part of the problem. Accuses these entities of abusing the country for “immense profit” due to the public allowing it. Acknowledgment of Complexity and Limitations:
Admits the problem is “more complex” and acknowledges not being “the most qualified person to lay out the full argument.” References to “Rosenthal” and “Moore” suggest that the author has been influenced by critics of the healthcare industry, possibly Elisabeth Rosenthal and Michael Moore, known for their work highlighting healthcare issues. Sense of Pioneering Action:
The concluding statement “Evidently I am the first to face it with such brutal honesty” implies a belief that they are taking unprecedented action to address these issues. Analysis:
Psychological Perspective:
The author appears to feel a strong moral imperative to act against perceived injustices within the healthcare system. There is a combination of frustration, disillusionment, and a desire for retribution. The language used suggests a potential disconnect from societal norms regarding acceptable methods of protest or activism. Motivation and Influences:
Deep dissatisfaction with the healthcare system, particularly the profit motives of large corporations. Influenced by existing critiques and literature on healthcare corruption and greed. A belief that traditional avenues for change are ineffective, prompting direct action. Potential Actions Taken:
While not explicitly stated, the use of terms like “social engineering,” “basic CAD,” and mention of causing “strife of traumas” implies that the author may have designed and executed a plan that could involve cyber activities, engineering sabotage, or other technical means to disrupt or damage targeted entities. The assertion of acting alone suggests a lone-wolf scenario, which can sometimes make detection and prevention more challenging. Implications for Investigation:
Authorities should consider the possibility of recent or imminent attacks against healthcare companies, particularly those involving technical expertise. The physical notebook mentioned could be a crucial piece of evidence containing plans, targets, or ideological writings. The author’s claim of secured technology indicates that digital forensics may be challenging but still essential. Recommendations:
Immediate Action:
Alert relevant law enforcement and cybersecurity teams to assess any current threats to healthcare companies, especially UnitedHealth Group. Review recent incidents for any correlations with the methods suggested. Investigation of Influences:
Examine works by Elisabeth Rosenthal and Michael Moore to understand the specific grievances that may have influenced the author. Analyze online forums, social media, and other communication channels for similar rhetoric or potential accomplices, despite the author’s claim of acting alone. Forensic Analysis:
Search for the physical spiral notebook referenced, which may contain critical information. Despite the author’s claims about secured technology, proceed with thorough digital investigations, as there may be recoverable data. Psychological and Behavioral Profiling:
Engage behavioral analysts or profilers to better understand the author’s mindset, which can aid in predicting future actions or identifying the individual. Look for individuals with engineering backgrounds who have expressed strong anti-healthcare system sentiments. Preventive Measures:
Advise healthcare organizations to enhance security protocols, both physical and cyber. Raise awareness among employees about social engineering tactics to prevent unauthorized access or manipulation. Conclusion:
The text is a serious and concerning communication that suggests premeditated actions taken against major entities within the U.S. healthcare system. The author’s combination of technical knowledge, ideological motivation, and apparent willingness to cause disruption or harm necessitates a prompt and coordinated response from authorities. Understanding the underlying motivations and potential methods is crucial for mitigating risks and preventing further incidents.
Disclaimer:
This analysis is based solely on the content provided and aims to offer an interpretation to assist in understanding potential implications. It should not be considered a definitive assessment, and further investigation would be required to corroborate any conclusions drawn.
I think the analysis is thought provoking and I especially appreciate how it invites further input from actual human experts in the relevant fields.

content:
Imagine applying for a job.
You have your CV, of course.
But you just know that you know so much more.
If you are in luck, some of what you know is written down somewhere. Maybe in a blog, maybe in documentation, maybe in articles.
And as soon is knowledge is written down, it is accessible to RAG - Retrieval-Augmented Generation
RAG is a method in natural language processing that combines retrieval and generation strategies to improve the quality and relevance of generated text.
It is also very handy for finding specific details relevant to some practical task at hand, such as writing a job application.
I have built custom RAGs in Nushell and in Python with LangChain, I’ve even built one on top of Simon Willison’s llm-rag .
But today I will use the RAG built-in to one of my favorite LLM command line tools, namely the rust-based aichat.
Let’s get to it:
First I start aichat in RAG-mode, naming the RAG-session simply job like so:
aichat -R job My aichat is currently set up with OpenAI - so aichat will ask me to choose from these embedding models:
? Select embedding model: > openai:text-embedding-3-large (max-tokens:8191;max-batch:100;price:0.13) openai:text-embedding-3-small (max-tokens:8191;max-batch:100;price:0.02) [↑↓ to move, enter to select, type to filter] In this case the external dataset (my blog) is rather small, and I like really snappy responses, so I will go with the smaller model.
aichat will then ask for chunk size and chunk overlay. I will go with the defaults.
Then it asks for the documents:
? Add documents: [e.g. file;dir/;dir/**/*.{md,mdx};solo-url;site-url/**] I will provide the English language blog here at Kiils.dk:
? Add documents: https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/** The two asterix at the end of the url are a wild-card, telling aichat to get all blog posts.
I then get this reply from aichat
Load https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/** [1/1] Start crawling url=https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/ exclude= extract= Crawled https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/ Crawled https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/2024-09-19-inspecting-yaml-frontmatter-in-markdown-files-with-nushell/ Crawled https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/chatgpt-glorified-markov-chain/ Crawled https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/2024-07-20-the-2-basic-workflows-for-ai-assisted-content-generation/ Crawled https://www.kiils.dk/en/blog/2024-06-03-get-items-from-rss-feed-with-nushell/ Crawled Welcome to aichat 0.23.0 Type ".help" for additional help. @job> Now, all of my blog posts in English at Kiils are stored as embeddings in this small knowledge database I just made.
And this means I can now do semantic search and find relevant information. I can simply search for content relevant to, in our example here, a specific job offer - and I can even write the search query in natural language, explaining the context carefully:
@job> I am applying for a job as an AI engineer with a focus on generative artificial intelligene, please give me relevant examples from the blog postings - you may elaborate on how exactly these are relevant for an AI engineer position at a company Then the RAG comes up with this answer:
—————— Here are some relevant examples from the blog postings that could be useful for an AI engineer position, particularly focused on generative artificial intelligence:
Marvin Library for AI Integration:
The blog discusses Marvin, a library for integrating AI into software, which can be likened to building various bots with unique AI personalities. For an AI engineer, understanding how to implement such libraries to integrate AI systems into codebases is critical, as it often involves creating efficient and effective solutions for utilizing large language models (LLMs). Embodying Humor in AI:
Another example is the challenge of making AI produce humor, tested through different emoji combinations and themes. This reflects the endeavor of creating generative AI models that can mimic human-like creativity and understand context, which is a valuable skill for fine-tuning and training models to fit specific human interactions or entertainment applications. Content Generation Workflows:
The blog mentions workflows in AI-assisted content creation, such as semi-automatic (LLM -> editor -> publication) and fully automatic (LLM -> publication) processes. An AI engineer should understand these workflows, their advantages and disadvantages, and how they are constructed and modified to enhance content quality and efficiency while leveraging LLM technology. BER Approach for AI Content:
The recipe of starting from a RAG-enhanced base, enriching with knowledge from LLMs, and then manually editing is significant. It shows the iterative process of enhancing AI-generated content, which is crucial for AI engineers who aim to optimize and personalize AI outputs. These examples highlight practical applications and challenges in using generative AI, which are highly relevant to the responsibilities of an AI engineer working in the field. Being able to understand, implement, and improve such systems is key to contributing effectively to a company that develops or utilizes generative AI technologies. ——————
Not bad.
I remember writing about workflows.
I remember coming up with the Base-Enrich-Reduce method, that I even helped to implement for a large Danish company in the car leasing industry.
I remember working with the MarvinAI Python library from Prefect, good stuff.
But what is “Embodying Humor in AI” about?
Let’s find out:
@job> In what blog posting did I employ humor with AI? —————— You employed humor with AI in the blog post titled “🦶 + 🥔 = Potato foot 🤣 - and other examples of how ChatGPT made my son laugh. And why it is important,” published on 22 May 2023. ——————
Ah yes, I remember now. We had such a good laugh. LLM’s can write extremely silly stuff humans would have a hard time coming up with :)
Anyway, as you can see, RAG can be used on your very own information. It can be very useful for doing what embeddings basically do, mapping semantic relations and giving meaningful answers.
In this case, to “resurface” what I have written of relevance to a particular job offering. And with the more general power of LLMs, to present this in a hopefully clear and convincing way in an application for the job.
And, as you can probably imagine, there are endless other ways to make use of this technology.
title: Using RAG when writing job applications

UPDATE jan 2026:
Nushell and the polars plugin have both evolved a lot since this was written.
The nushell polars plugin code below must be updated like so:
def bible [] { let corp = open --raw bible.txt | str downcase | split words | polars into-df let stop = [i a an and are as at be by for from how in is it of on or that the this to was what when where who will with the] let tidy = $corp | polars with-column (polars col 0 | polars is-in $stop | polars as wordin) | polars filter ((polars col wordin) == false ) | polars drop wordin let freq = $tidy | polars value-counts let sort = $freq | polars sort-by count $sort } The performance is still at the same awesome level 🚀
Word frequency analysis is important in quantitative text analysis.
Nushell has a plugin for Polars support.
When installed, you can analyse a large corpus of text very fast:
def bible [] { let corp = open --raw /home/lk/Data/king-james-bible.txt | str downcase | split words | polars into-df let stop = [i a an and are as at be by for from how in is it of on or that the this to was what when where who will with the] | polars into-df let mask = $corp | polars is-in $stop let tidy = $corp | polars filter-with ($mask | polars not) let freq = $tidy | polars value-counts let sort = $freq | polars sort-by count $sort } Giving:
╭───────┬────────────┬───────╮ │ # │ 0 │ count │ ├───────┼────────────┼───────┤ │ 0 │ endow │ 1 │ │ 1 │ clappeth │ 1 │ │ 2 │ elishaphat │ 1 │ │ 3 │ muse │ 1 │ │ 4 │ makaz │ 1 │ │ 5 │ swimmeth │ 1 │ │ 6 │ fidelity │ 1 │ │ 7 │ jeziah │ 1 │ │ 8 │ savours │ 1 │ │ 9 │ ashvath │ 1 │ │ ... │ ... │ ... │ │ 13019 │ all │ 5637 │ │ 13020 │ them │ 6430 │ │ 13021 │ not │ 6624 │ │ 13022 │ him │ 6659 │ │ 13023 │ they │ 7378 │ │ 13024 │ lord │ 7964 │ │ 13025 │ his │ 8473 │ │ 13026 │ unto │ 8997 │ │ 13027 │ shall │ 9840 │ │ 13028 │ he │ 10422 │ ╰───────┴────────────┴───────╯ And it took less than a second.
To be specific: 444ms 413µs 290ns.
Doing the same in “vanilla” Nushell like so:
def biblenu [] { let corp = open --raw /home/lk/Data/king-james-bible.txt | str downcase | split words | wrap corp let stop = [i a an and are as at be by for from how in is it of on or that the this to was what when where who will with the] | wrap stop let tidy = $corp | where corp in $stop.stop == false let freq = $tidy | uniq --count let sort = $freq | sort-by count $sort | flatten } gives
│ 13019 │ all │ 5637 │ │ 13020 │ them │ 6430 │ │ 13021 │ not │ 6624 │ │ 13022 │ him │ 6659 │ │ 13023 │ they │ 7378 │ │ 13024 │ lord │ 7964 │ │ 13025 │ his │ 8473 │ │ 13026 │ unto │ 8997 │ │ 13027 │ shall │ 9840 │ │ 13028 │ he │ 10422 │ ├───────┼───────┼───────┤ │ # │ corp │ count │ ╰───────┴───────┴───────╯ So the same result.
But this time it took: 4sec 118ms 703µs 223ns
So Nushell with Polars is around 10x faster for this kind of task than Nushell without Polars.
title: Analysing the entire Holy Bible in less than a second

content:
Markdown is widely used when working with text based generative artificial intelligence.
YAML is suitable for more structured data.
The two can be combined as follows.
--- title: Blog about Nushell and structured data date: 2024-09-19 tags: - Nushell - data --- The body text goes here. Imagine the above text is in a file called blog-1.md
The part between the --- lines is the frontmatter in YAML. Everything below the second --- line is the markdown content.
Then in Nushell I create a small custom command like so:
def frontmatter [] { lines | split list '---' | do { |lst| let fm = $lst.0 | to text | from yaml | into value | into record { frontmatter: $fm content: ($lst | skip 1 | to text | str trim) } } $in } With this I can do:
open blog-1.md | frontmatter And I get
╭─────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ │ ╭───────┬────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ │ frontmatter │ │ title │ Blog about Nushell and structured data │ │ │ │ │ date │ 11 hours ago │ │ │ │ │ │ ╭───┬─────────╮ │ │ │ │ │ tags │ │ 0 │ Nushell │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ 1 │ data │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ╰───┴─────────╯ │ │ │ │ ╰───────┴────────────────────────────────────────╯ │ │ content │ The body text goes here. │ ╰─────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ This can be used in other pipelines, eg. when publishing
let body = open $path | frontmatter | get content let meta = open $path | frontmatter | get frontmatter But also for finding, for example, posts that are not yet published:
open *.md | each { frontmatter } | get frontmatter | where draft == true and slightly more complicated things like finding the most frequently used tags:
glob **/*.md | par-each { open $in | frontmatter | get frontmatter.tools? } | flatten | uniq -c | sort-by count giving
╭────┬───────────┬───────╮ │ # │ value │ count │ ├────┼───────────┼───────┤ │ 0 │ latex │ 1 │ │ 1 │ fontforge │ 1 │ │ 2 │ groff │ 1 │ │ 3 │ LLM │ 1 │ │ 4 │ Nushell │ 1 │ │ 5 │ markdown │ 1 │ │ 6 │ Marvin │ 1 │ │ 7 │ drupal │ 1 │ │ 8 │ pandoc │ 2 │ │ 9 │ llm │ 2 │ │ 10 │ nvim │ 3 │ │ 11 │ aichat │ 3 │ │ 12 │ ChatGPT │ 4 │ │ 13 │ Nushell │ 13 │ ╰────┴───────────┴───────╯ Note the ? after .tools in the above command. This is because not all my markdown files has a tools key in the frontmatter. When ? is used, files without the tools key will just be ignored instead of breaking the pipeline.
Much, much more can be done with this of course. Not least combining it with LLMs.
Final note:
Doing
glob **/*.md | par-each { open $in | frontmatter }
is more robust than
open **/*.md | par-each { frontmatter }
when some files have lots of weird characters in them.
title: Inspecting yaml frontmatter in markdown files with Nushell

content:
Fundamentally LLMs are all about relating text to text.
An LLM can complete, enrich or predict text by relating input text from the user to all the text relations already in the models interior.
The person working with an LLM will want to benefit from its power and vast “knowledge” of language.
Nushell is the best way I have found to do this in a way that is both systematic and, once you have learned the basics of Nushell, easy and straight forward.
Let us have a look at an example. We have this table in Nushell:
name age hobbies Alice 30 reading Bob 25 gaming Charlie 35 photography Diana 28 painting Ethan 22 writing We want to create a small fiction about each of these persons.
In Nushell then simply do:
$table | insert fiction { $in | aichat provide very short fiction based on input } As you may have noticed I also use the terrific CLI tool AIChat
Back to our example, we now have this:
name age hobbies fiction Alice 30 reading Alice sat in her favorite nook, surrounded by towering stacks of novels. The scent of old pages filled the air as she flipped through a worn paperback, completely absorbed. Outside, the world buzzed, but within her pages, she traveled to distant lands and met captivating characters. One day, lost in a particularly gripping story, she stumbled upon a mystical map tucked between the chapters. It pulsed with an otherworldly glow. Curiosity igniting, she followed its path, embarking on an adventure beyond her wildest dreams. As she stepped into the world of the book, she realized that in every story, magic awaits those brave enough to read between the lines. Bob 25 gaming In a bustling city, Bob, a 25-year-old gaming enthusiast, discovered a virtual realm where skills blurred reality. One fateful night, while battling a fearsome dragon, he unlocked a glitch—a portal that transported him into the digital landscape. Surrounded by pixelated wonders, Bob no longer had to worry about his mundane job. He wielded a sword forged from the essence of code, joined by allies he'd only dreamt of. With each victory, he felt alive, more than ever before, but a nagging question lingered: could he return to his world, or was this new home where he truly belonged? As the sun set over the glowing horizon, Bob looked back at the portal, the flickering light a reminder of the life he almost left behind. With a deep breath, he stepped forward into the adventure ahead. Charlie 35 photography Charlie adjusted the lens on his camera, the early morning light dancing through the trees. He captured the world in frames, each click telling a story only he could see. One day, while wandering through a forgotten garden, he stumbled upon a faded photograph half-buried in the dirt. It showed a smiling girl with wildflowers in her hair, her eyes sparkling with joy. Intrigued, Charlie wanted to know her story. As he printed the photo, he noticed a date scribbled on the back—exactly fifty years ago. With each passing moment, he felt a connection, as if the girl was guiding him. Driven by curiosity, he set out to find her, believing that somewhere in the world, magic still lingered among the forgotten memories, waiting for someone to uncover them. Diana 28 painting Diana stood before her easel, the fading light of the day streaming through the window. Each brushstroke whispered secrets of a world only she could see. As she painted, colors melded and flowed, reflecting not just landscapes, but her dreams, hopes, and fears. Today, she tackled a piece she’d long envisioned—a towering oak nestled amidst a field of wildflowers. With each hue, memories flooded back: laughter shared under the sprawling branches, quiet afternoons spent in thoughtful solitude. As the final details emerged, an inexplicable sense of peace washed over her. In that moment, Diana realized that through painting, she wasn't just creating art; she was capturing the essence of her own life, boldly framed in vibrant colors and the rich aroma of oil paint. Ethan 22 writing Ethan sat in the dim light of his cramped studio apartment, fingers poised over the keyboard. The scent of stale coffee lingered in the air as he wrestled with his latest story—a tale where words danced like shadows in the moonlight. At 22, his dreams were woven with ink, stretching beyond the walls that confined him. Characters whispered their secrets, pulling him deeper into worlds yet unexplored. He wrote not for fame, but for the heartbeat of creation, and tonight, the pulse of a new adventure throbbed in his veins. As the clock ticked ominously toward midnight, the first sentence spilled forth, igniting the night with infinite possibilities. Ethan smiled, lost in his thoughts, because in the realm of fiction, he could always be more than just a struggling writer. Tonight, he would conquer galaxies. In the above example we asked Nushell to relate each whole row to the LLM with the $in variable.
If we instead want to relate just one cell from each row, this can easily be done like so:
$table | insert description { $in.hobbies | aichat provide very short one paragraph description of the hobby } Notice the $in.hobbies - only feeding each hobby cell in the table to the LLM this time around.
Let us “save” the result in a new table, though:
let hobby = $table | insert description { $in.hobbies | aichat provide very short one paragraph description of the hobby } Giving us this:
name age hobbies description Alice 30 reading Reading is a captivating hobby that involves immersing oneself in written words, whether through books, articles, or poetry, to explore new ideas, cultures, and perspectives. It fosters imagination and critical thinking, allowing individuals to escape reality, learn, and grow. Moreover, reading can be a solitary pleasure or a shared experience, connecting people through discussions and book clubs, making it a versatile and enriching pastime. Bob 25 gaming Gaming is a popular hobby that involves playing video games across various platforms, including consoles, PCs, and mobile devices. It offers immersive experiences through interactive storytelling, competitive challenges, and social interaction with other players, whether locally or online. With a diverse range of genres—such as action, adventure, role-playing, and simulation—gaming appeals to people of all ages and backgrounds, fostering creativity, strategic thinking, and community engagement. Charlie 35 photography Photography is the art and practice of capturing light to create images, allowing individuals to express their creativity, document moments, and explore the world around them. With various styles ranging from landscapes and portraits to street photography and macro, it combines technical skills with artistic vision, enabling enthusiasts to convey stories and emotions through the lens. Whether using a professional camera or a smartphone, photography offers a rewarding way to observe and share the beauty in everyday life. Diana 28 painting Painting is a creative hobby that involves applying pigment to a surface, such as canvas, paper, or wood, to express emotions, ideas, or beauty. It allows individuals to explore their imagination and artistic skills, using various techniques and mediums like watercolors, acrylics, or oils. Whether for relaxation, personal expression, or social engagement, painting offers a fulfilling way to create visually captivating works and can be enjoyed by people of all ages and skill levels. Ethan 22 writing Writing is a creative hobby that involves expressing thoughts, ideas, and stories through written words. It can take many forms, including poetry, fiction, nonfiction, blogging, and journaling, allowing individuals to explore their imagination, share personal experiences, or convey information. Whether for personal enjoyment, therapeutic reasons, or the aspiration to publish, writing offers a fulfilling way to articulate one’s voice and connect with others. In case we are only interested in the hobby descriptions, Nushell makes it very easy to select only that column like so:
$hobby | select description description Reading is a captivating hobby that involves immersing oneself in written words, whether through books, articles, or poetry, to explore new ideas, cultures, and perspectives. It fosters imagination and critical thinking, allowing individuals to escape reality, learn, and grow. Moreover, reading can be a solitary pleasure or a shared experience, connecting people through discussions and book clubs, making it a versatile and enriching pastime. Gaming is a popular hobby that involves playing video games across various platforms, including consoles, PCs, and mobile devices. It offers immersive experiences through interactive storytelling, competitive challenges, and social interaction with other players, whether locally or online. With a diverse range of genres—such as action, adventure, role-playing, and simulation—gaming appeals to people of all ages and backgrounds, fostering creativity, strategic thinking, and community engagement. Photography is the art and practice of capturing light to create images, allowing individuals to express their creativity, document moments, and explore the world around them. With various styles ranging from landscapes and portraits to street photography and macro, it combines technical skills with artistic vision, enabling enthusiasts to convey stories and emotions through the lens. Whether using a professional camera or a smartphone, photography offers a rewarding way to observe and share the beauty in everyday life. … and so on.
I need to 🏊 now. But remember, I’ve only just scratched the surface here.
The possibilities for relating text, specific parts of texts and text-based structured data to the immense power of LLMs with Nushell are almost endless.
You can read more about Nushell here: Nushell · Kiils
Also make sure to visit the Nushell homepage here: Nushell
title: Why Nushell is so BRILLIANT at working with AI

content:
It depends.
When creating a complex piece of content from many sources, it is often best to keep input in one Nushell table and place the output in another.
When creating many smaller and simpler pieces of content it is often much more efficient to place the output as separate columns in the input table. In many of these cases the input and the output will naturally belong on the same row.
For more complicated workflows that do not fit into either of the aforementioned categories, you may in some case benefit from joining input and output tables in various ways.
In general, it is best to have a simple workflow that you can easily comprehend and navigate. You do not want too many interconnected moving parts in different places.
title: Should I keep input and output separate when doing AI-assisted content generation in Nushell

content:
De to grundlæggende typer af arbejdsgange for indholdsskabelse, når man arbejder med LLM’er, er disse:
Semi-automatisk
LLM -> redaktør -> publikation
Fuldstændig automatisk
LLM -> publikation
Der kan selvfølgelig være forskellige trin før, mellem og efter behandlingen med kode i begge.
Men her fokuserer jeg på, om et menneske er involveret i workflowet for indholdsskabelse eller ej.
Lad os først se på fordelene ved begge tilgange:
Fordele # Fuldautomatisk arbejdsgang Halvautomatisk arbejdsgang Hastighed - Processer kan gennemføres hurtigt uden menneskelig indgriben. Kvalitetskontrol - Menneskelige redaktører kan sikre højere nøjagtighed og kvalitet ved at gribe ind, når det er nødvendigt. Konsistens - Outputtet er ensartet uden subjektiv variation. Fleksibilitet - Tilpasninger kan foretages on-the-fly baseret på redaktørens indsigt eller ekstern feedback. Skalerbarhed - Let at skalere operationer til at håndtere store mængder opgaver uden yderligere omkostninger til menneskelige ressourcer. Fejlkorrektion - Menneskelig indsigt giver mulighed for øjeblikkelig identifikation og korrektion af fejl, som måske ville blive overset af automatiserede systemer. Omkostningseffektivitet - Reducerer lønomkostningerne forbundet med manuelle opgaver over lange perioder. Kritisk tænkning - Mennesker kan anvende nuanceret dømmekraft, som er vanskelig for automatiserede systemer at replikere, især i komplekse scenarier. 24/7 tilgængelighed - Kan fungere kontinuerligt uden pauser eller nedetid, som mennesker har brug for. Procesforbedring - Menneskelig indgriben sikrer øjeblikkelig feedback på workflow-resultater, hvilket forbedrer processerne over tid. Og hvad er så ulemperne?
Ulemper # Fuldautomatisk arbejdsgang Halvautomatisk arbejdsgang Mangel på fleksibilitet - Kæmper med at håndtere undtagelser eller uventede situationer, der ikke er forprogrammerede. Langsommere processer - Inddragelse af menneskelige redaktører kan gøre workflowet langsommere sammenlignet med fuldautomatiske systemer. Begrænset forståelse - Fortolker måske ikke komplekse eller nuancerede oplysninger lige så effektivt som et menneske. Højere omkostninger - Kræver løbende investering i menneskelige ressourcer, hvilket kan være dyrere end fuldautomatiske løsninger. Afhængighed af datakvalitet - Ydeevnen er stærkt afhængig af kvaliteten og bredden af inputdataene. Uoverensstemmelse - Menneskelig indgriben kan medføre variationer i outputkvaliteten afhængigt af den enkelte redaktørs færdigheder og vurderinger. Ingen personlig kontakt - Kan ikke levere de menneskelignende interaktioner eller beslutninger, der kan være nødvendige inden for nogle områder som f.eks. kundeservice. Skalerbarhedsproblemer - Opskalering indebærer yderligere uddannelse og ansættelse, hvilket kan være dyrt og tidskrævende. Overdreven afhængighed af teknologi - Kan føre til reducerede færdigheder blandt personalet og en overdreven afhængighed af automatiserede systemer. Træthed og fejl - Menneskelige redaktører kan begå fejl, især når de håndterer gentagne opgaver eller arbejder under pres. Som altid kan man ikke få det hele. Der er ulemper ved begge teknikker.
I virkeligheden er det godt at skifte frem og tilbage mellem de to workflowtyper, især i udviklingsfasen, for at høste fordelene og indsigterne fra begge.
Det siger sig selv, at nogle opgaver med at skabe indhold er mere velegnede til fuld automatisering, mens andre kræver menneskeligt tilsyn.
title: De 2 fundamentale arbejdsgange for ai-assisteret indhold

content:
The two basic kinds of content creation workflows when working with LLMs are these:
Semi-automatic
LLM -> editor -> publication
Fully automatic
LLM -> publication
Of course there can be various -pre, -in between and -post processing steps by code in either.
But here I focus on whether a human is involved in the content creation workflow or not.
First, let’s have a look at the advantages of either approach:
Advantages # Fully Automatic Workflow Semi-Automatic Workflow Speed - Processes can be completed rapidly without human intervention. Quality Control - Human editors can ensure higher accuracy and quality by intervening when necessary. Consistency - Outputs are uniform without any subjective variation. Flexibility - Adaptations can be made on-the-fly based on editor insights or external feedback. Scalability - Easy to scale operations to handle large volumes of tasks without additional human resource costs. Error Correction - Human insight allows for immediate error identification and correction, which might be overlooked by automated systems. Cost Efficiency - Reduces labor costs associated with manual tasks over long periods. Critical Thinking - Humans can apply nuanced judgment that is difficult for automated systems to replicate, especially in complex scenarios. 24/7 Availability - Can operate continuously without breaks or downtime needed by humans. Process Improvement- Human intervention secures immediate feedback on workflow results, improving processes over time. And then, what are the disadvantages?
Disadvantages # Fully Automatic Workflow Semi-Automatic Workflow Lack of Flexibility - Struggles with handling exceptions or unexpected situations that are not pre-programmed. Slower Processes - Involvement of human editors can slow down the workflow compared to fully automated systems. Limited Understanding - May not interpret complex or nuanced information as effectively as a human. Higher Costs - Requires ongoing investment in human resources, which can be more expensive than fully automated solutions. Dependency on Data Quality - Performance heavily reliant on the quality and breadth of the input data. Inconsistency - Human intervention might introduce variability in the output quality depending on the individual editor’s skills and judgments. No Personal Touch - Unable to provide the human-like interactions or decisions that might be necessary in some fields like customer service. Scalability Issues - Scaling up involves additional training and hiring, which can be costly and time-consuming. Over-reliance on Technology - Can lead to reduced skills among staff and an over-dependence on automated systems. Fatigue and Errors - Human editors can make mistakes, especially when handling repetitive tasks or working under pressure. As always you cannot have it all. There are trade offs to both techniques.
In reality it is good to switch back and forth between to the two workflow types especially during the development phase to reap the awards and insights of both.
It goes without saying that some content creation tasks are more suited for full automatization while others require human oversight.
title: The 2 basic workflows for ai-assisted content generation

content:
So I want to publish a listicle on my website.
It just so happens that listicles are among the content genres that are most effectively and convincingly assisted in their creation by generative artificial intelligence. I could explain why this is, but in this blog I will instead show you how to create a listicle and publish it - all without ever leaving your shell 🤭.
If you need ideas for listicles, I am sure GAI can help you with that too. I got the idea from my sons now former interest in the strange spectacle of wrestling.
And I am a little curious about these colorful personalities myself.
First, get the list of the best wrestlers.
For this I have coded my own Nushell custom command which uses "response_format":{"type":"json_object"}, which aichat does not. This allows me to cleanly get just the list items (the values) themselves, every time. No exceptions.
def lls [ ...prompt: string ] { if ($in | is-empty) and ($prompt | is-empty) { 'Please provide input' } else { let prompt = ( if not ($in | is-empty) and not ($prompt | is-empty) { ($prompt | str join ' ') ++ ' ' ++ $in } else if not ($in | is-empty) and ($prompt | is-empty) { $in } else { ($prompt | str join ' ') } ) let system = "Output valid json." let payload = {"model":"gpt-3.5-turbo-0125", "response_format":{"type":"json_object"}, "messages":[{"role":"system","content":$system}, {"role":"user","content":$prompt}]} print 'Samlet prompt: ' $prompt "\n" let response = (http post --content-type application/json --full --headers [Content-Type application/json Authorization $"Bearer ($env.OPENAI_API_KEY)"] https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions $payload ) $response | get body.choices.message.content.0 | from json | values | flatten | flatten | flatten | tee { to json | wl-copy } } } Running lls greatest wrestlers of all time list then gives
[ "Hulk Hogan", "The Rock", "Stone Cold Steve Austin", "John Cena", "Ric Flair", "Shawn Michaels", "Undertaker", "Bret Hart", "Macho Man Randy Savage", "Andre the Giant" ] I’ll just trust Sam Altman here, since I do not posses the knowledge to evaluate the list myself. So onwards with this list of GOATs in wrestling.
The next step is to enrich the list with a brief description of each subject on the list. I do this like so:
let enriched = p | from json | wrap subject | insert description { aichat short description of $in.subject } (I wish commands like insert, upsert and update could run in parallel like par-each can, but I currently do not think that is possible. See also Speeding up ai-assisted content generation with Nushell par-each · Kiils)
In json the enriched variable then looks something like:
[ { "subject": "Hulk Hogan", "description": "Hulk Hogan, born Terry Eugene Bollea on August 11, 1953, is an iconic American professional wrestler, television personality, actor, and musician. He gained worldwide fame in the 1980s and 1990s as the face of World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE), becoming one of the most popular and recognizable figures in wrestling history. Known for his charismatic personality, signature moves, and catchphrases like \"Hulkamania\" and \"Whatcha gonna do brother?\", Hogan has a lasting legacy in the world of sports entertainment." }, { "subject": "The Rock", "description": "Dwayne \"The Rock\" Johnson is an American actor, producer, and former professional wrestler. He gained fame as a WWE superstar before transitioning to a successful film career. Known for his charismatic personality and impressive physique, The Rock has starred in blockbuster movies such as the \"Fast & Furious\" series, \"Jumanji,\" and \"Moana.\" He is also a notable philanthropist and entrepreneur." }, { "subject": "Stone Cold Steve Austin", "description": "Stone Cold Steve Austin, born Steven James Anderson, is a retired professional wrestler and actor who gained iconic status in the WWE during the late 1990s and early 2000s. Known for his rebellious anti-authority persona, Austin became a fan favorite with his trademark \"Austin 3:16\" catchphrase, intense in-ring style, and memorable feuds with Vince McMahon and other top superstars. He is one of the most popular and influential wrestlers in history, contributing significantly to WWE's \"Attitude Era.\"" }, ... These descriptions confirm my suspicion that the best wrestlers are all highly entertaining personalities, as much as great athletes, if not more so.
This I then “convert” to markdown like so
let md = $enriched | each { $"\n## ($in.subject)\n\n($in.description)\n" } | to text giving
## Hulk Hogan Hulk Hogan, born Terry Eugene Bollea on August 11, 1953, is an iconic American professional wrestler, television personality, actor, and musician. He gained worldwide fame in the 1980s and 1990s as the face of World Wrestling Federation (WWF, now WWE), becoming one of the most popular and recognizable figures in wrestling history. Known for his charismatic personality, signature moves, and catchphrases like "Hulkamania" and "Whatcha gonna do brother?", Hogan has a lasting legacy in the world of sports entertainment. ## The Rock Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson is an American actor, producer, and former professional wrestler. He gained fame as a WWE superstar before transitioning to a successful film career. Known for his charismatic personality and impressive physique, The Rock has starred in blockbuster movies such as the "Fast & Furious" series, "Jumanji," and "Moana." He is also a notable philanthropist and entrepreneur. ## Stone Cold Steve Austin Stone Cold Steve Austin, born Steven James Anderson, is a retired professional wrestler and actor who gained iconic status in the WWE during the late 1990s and early 2000s. ... Then I edit this manually.
Next step is to ready the text for publishing on a drupal site. So I embed the markdown in json. And either manually or with ai assistance provide a title, and finally move the title before the content (only for my own viewing convenience)
let jsontc = $md | to json | wrap content | insert title { 'GOATs and OGs of wrestling' } | select title content giving
╭─────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ title │ GOATs and OGs of wrestling │ │ content │ "\n## Hulk Hogan\n\nHulk Hogan, born Terry Eugene Bollea on August │ │ │ 11, 1953, is an iconic American professional wrestler, television │ │ │ personality, actor, and musician. He gained worldwide fame in the │ │ │ 1980s and 1990s as the face of World Wrestling Federation (WWF, │ │ │ now WWE), becoming one of the most popular and recognizable │ │ │ figures in wrestling history. Known for his charismatic │ │ │ personality, signature moves, and catchphrases like \"Hulkamania\" │ │ │ and \"Whatcha gonna do brother?\", Hogan has a lasting legacy in │ Now we need to get the payload for the drupal jsonapi ready:
let payload = ( $jsontc | par-each { ( { "data": { "type": "node--listicle", "attributes": { "title": $jsontc.title, "body": { "value": ($jsontc.content | from json | pandoc --from markdown --to html), "format": "ckeditor5" } }, "relationships": { "uid": { "data": { "type": "user--user", "id": 7d137122-c5f9-4313-b417-4a97cd5ba79f } }, } } } ) } ) The payload looks like this now:
╭──────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ │ ╭───────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ │ data │ │ type │ node--listicle │ │ │ │ │ │ ╭───────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ │ │ │ │ attributes │ │ title │ GOATs and OGs of wrestling │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ ╭────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ body │ │ value │ <h2 id="hulk-hogan">Hulk Hogan</h2> │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ <p>Hulk Hogan, │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ born Terry Eugene Bollea on August 11, 1953, is an │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ iconic │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ American professional wrestler, television │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ personality, actor, and │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ │ musician. He gained │ │ │ │ which is what drupal expects.
Now all that is left is to send it to the drupal site:
( http post --content-type application/json --headers [Content-type application/vnd.api+json] --headers [Accept application/vnd.api+json] --user 'Lennart Kiil' --password 'password here' https://www.folkets.dk/jsonapi/node/listicle $payload ) | from json And now the listicle is online. In fact, you can read the translated, in Danish, version here:
GOATs and OGs of wrestling
PS. I forgot to mention, I also use pandoc in the above example. Pandoc is a great tool for converting between various text formats like html, markdown, plain and many more.
title: Creating a listicle with Nushell and aichat and publishing it on a drupal site

Given this json list of wrestlers
[ "Hulk Hogan", "Stone Cold Steve Austin", "The Rock", "Ric Flair", "Andre the Giant", "Shawn Michaels", "John Cena", "The Undertaker", "Bret Hart", "Macho Man Randy Savage" ] the goal was simple.
Create a brief description of each wrestler.
In Nushell that can be done in various ways. Two of which are:
from json | par-each --threads 10 { aichat short description of $in } and
from json | each { aichat short description of $in } The first one will make parallel requests to the openAI api.
The second one will make the requests one by one in serial.
The first one is about 8 times faster than the second one in this experiment.
